articles.title_orig: Russia, Ukraine agree to ceasefire in Ukrainian city hit by food crisis, brokered by Melania Trump
articles.title_zh: Russia, Ukraine agree to ceasefire in Ukrainian city hit by food crisis, brokered by Melania Trump
articles.content_orig:
People in Russian-occupied city facing severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with some reportedly surviving on weeds
The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive.
In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians.
Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations.
Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.
The White House statement said the ceasefire was brokered by Melania Trump , and her representative worked directly with ​Russian and Ukrainian ‌leadership to define the ​terms. “Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” the first lady said.
Despite the claim the ceasefire had been brokered by Melania Trump, there had already been protracted efforts to organise a humanitarian ceasefire, with claims by Ukrainian officials that it had been Russia that had rejected previous calls.
Calls for a ceasefire had been issued by Pope Leo XIV – who discussed the issue with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – the United Nations, EU officials and the Council of Europe . As recently as 18 October, Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, had also said he thought agreement was close without any mention of the first lady’s involvement.
Ukraine has for weeks been pushing for a civilian evacuation from Oleshky and nearby settlements, at times using drones to airdrop emergency food and medical supplies into town.
Lubinets ⁠told Reuters on Friday that the mission to Oleshky would involve ⁠demining roads leading into the town, delivering food and evacuating civilians. “A sufficient ​quantity of ‌humanitarian ‌aid will be delivered to ‌meet the needs of everyone who requires it. What’s more, we are working to ensure ‌that this is not just a ​one-off event, and that it is not limited to Oleshky alone,” ⁠he said.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces continue to report widespread disruptions to the Starlink satellite network , despite Donald Trump’s claim that Elon Musk had lifted restrictions on the service.
The slowdown, which has affected the communications system used by Ukrainian troops, began last week after Trump and Elon Musk, the founder of Starlink, publicly criticised Zelenskyy over continued strikes on Russian oil refineries.
The restrictions have raised questions and confusion about who ordered the slowdown and why, with Trump and Musk denying responsibility. Asked about the Starlink slowdowns on Friday, Trump said he would speak to Musk if the restrictions remained in place.
“I’ve heard it was fixed, but if it’s not, I’ll speak to him,” he told reporters.
Ukrainian officials said throughout the day on Friday that speeds remained capped at about 100mph, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted.
“At present, we have not observed any lifting of the restrictions on Starlink,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Zelenskyy.
“There have been isolated cases in which Starlink has operated at speeds slightly above the imposed limits, but this is likely due to SpaceX’s algorithms or specific conditions of use, rather than any lifting of the restrictions,” Beskrestnov added.
after newsletter promotion
The speed restrictions have prevented Ukrainian military equipment, including drones, from maintaining a connection to the satellite network when travelling at high speeds, hampering offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept incoming Russian attacks.
The slowing down of Starlink, coupled with Zelenskyy’s complaints that Washington had temporarily suspended intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, has plunged relations between Ukraine and the US to a new low in recent days.
Tensions first flared after Washington’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel , as Trump sought to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections. Maritime tracking data showed that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was en route to New York on Thursday.
Meanwhile, Russia launched another overnight barrage against Ukraine, even as Moscow said a fresh round of US-brokered talks aimed at ending the war could take place next month.
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Friday that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US were expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in November. Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to produce a breakthrough, with Moscow and Kyiv far away over the terms of any peace settlement.
Among Russia’s maximalist demands are that Ukraine withdraw its forces from territory it still controls in the east of the country, drastically reduce the size of its military and adopt a neutral status that would rule out Nato membership.
Speaking to a Russian state television reporter late on Thursday, Putin once again questioned Ukraine’s sovereignty, echoing claims he has repeatedly made throughout the war. “The lands lost by Kyiv are not their territory, they are Russia’s historical lands,” Putin said.
The Russian president also cited unspecified genetic research to revive his longstanding claim that Russians and Ukrainians were “one people”, before insisting that Moscow would achieve all the objectives of its full-scale invasion.

articles.title_orig: Meghan ‘deeply distressed’ by report alleging her dad possessed child sexual abuse images
articles.title_zh: Meghan ‘deeply distressed’ by report alleging her dad possessed child sexual abuse images
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex , said Friday that she was “deeply distressed” by a report alleging that her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr. , possessed child sexual abuse images, adding that she was informed by police of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018.
In a statement Friday, Meghan addressed the report that her father was being investigated over claims he kept child sexual abuse videos and images at his home in the Philippines. “The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” said Meghan, who has in recent years had a limited and fraught relationship with her father. He did not attend her wedding to Prince Harry in 2018, drawing widespread media scrutiny.
The allegations against Markle Sr. were first reported Thursday by The Sun newspaper, a British tabloid, which reported that his son had informed police after he said he found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s home. The Sun published a photo it said showed his son, Thomas  Markle Jr., signing a sworn statement it said he had submitted to police and quoted him as saying: “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.”
Markle Sr., 82, denied the reported allegations, calling them “sick lies” in a statement to Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper. He added they were “the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”
NBC News was not immediately able to identify a contact for  Markle Sr., who the Daily Mail reported was now in a Florida rehab center recovering from surgery.
Markle Jr. told the Sun that he had reported his discovery to the FBI, as well as local Philippine authorities. NBC News has reached out to the FBI for comment, which did not immediately respond.
The Philippines’ justice department confirmed Friday that “the matter is under investigation” but otherwise declined to “provide further details at this time.”
Police in Cebu City, the location of Markle Sr.’s home in the Philippines, and London’s Metropolitan Police did not immediately respond to requests for comment from NBC News.
In the rare statement Friday, Meghan said that she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.”
“I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed,” she said in the statement.
Meghan said that she had been made aware of a letter sent to the British police and other authorities in 2018, that “made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.”
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” she added.
“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” Meghan said.
Asked by NBC News when Meghan was made aware of the letter to the Metropolitan Police, a spokesman for the couple said it was in the summer of 2018, after her wedding with Harry.
Separately, a source close to the couple told NBC News that Meghan’s decision not to speak publicly eight years ago should be understood in a particular context: “When she was made aware of these allegations in 2018 after they were reported to the police, they remained just that — allegations.”
“To have repeated them publicly at that stage would not only have potentially exposed her to civil action for making unsubstantiated claims, but she had also been advised that doing so could jeopardize any subsequent investigation,” the source added.
Markle Sr. told the Daily Mail he had not spoken to his son “for months” and said “these terrible lies are being made against me with no proof.” He added that he would “welcome an investigation” into the matter and labeled the accusations “a bunch of lies.”
His daughter, Samantha Markle, also told the Daily Mail of her brother’s allegations: “there is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever ... He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”
NBC News did not immediately receive responses to requests for comment from Markle Jr. or Samantha Markle — Meghan’s half-siblings.
Markle Sr. married Meghan’s mother, Doria Ragland, in 1979 and they subsequently divorced in 1987.
Meghan, 45, and Harry, 42, moved back to the United Kingdom earlier this summer after several years in the United States.
The couple made their first joint public appearance last week visiting charities in central England. King Charles III has made clear that their return does not signal a return to active royal life. Harry, however, has said recently that he wants his disagreements with his family to “work out.”
Adela Suliman is a breaking-news editor and reporter for NBC News in London.

articles.title_orig: Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
articles.title_zh: Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
articles.content_orig:
According to the new terms, sharing your data for better AI recommendations also means opening it up for more personalized ads.
According to the new terms, sharing your data for better AI recommendations also means opening it up for more personalized ads.
Google has updated its privacy policy in a way that could mean you’ll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you’re using personalized AI features. The update, spotted by Android Authority , adds an exception to its promise about not using your Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos for personalized ads. While the previous version simply said it wouldn’t do that, as of October 16th, Google has added the line, “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.”
That means anyone who has connected their Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos to AI Mode and other Search tools via Google’s Personal Intelligence feature — allowing those tools to provide better responses or recommendations by knowing more about you — may now see ads targeted on the basis of that content.
Advertisers don’t get access to your Drive, Gmail, and Photos information or personally identifying details such as your name or email address, and Google won’t show you ads based on sensitive categories like race, sexual orientation, religion, or health.
This is what the policy says:
“You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service. For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.”
“Depending on your settings, we may also show you personalized ads based on your interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services. For example, if you search for ‘mountain bikes,’ in Search you may see ads for sports equipment on YouTube.”
If you want to prevent your personal data from being used for targeted ads, you can choose which apps you want to disconnect from Search’s Personal Intelligence features or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings page.

articles.title_orig: Trump Blasts Vanity Fair Over ‘Fake News’ On Jared Kushner’s Alleged Undisclosed Foreign Bank Accounts
articles.title_zh: Trump Blasts Vanity Fair Over ‘Fake News’ On Jared Kushner’s Alleged Undisclosed Foreign Bank Accounts
articles.content_orig:
In late spring 2020, a source I knew to be reliable called me with a story. The Dutch government had hacked into Jared Kushner ’s phone and monitored him as he accessed a Dubai-based bank account. What was odd, the source said, was that the money in the account—hundreds of millions of dollars—had come from a bank in Azerbaijan. Most importantly, Kushner appeared to have transferred significant amounts of money from the Dubai account to other individuals, including a warlord, a mercenary and a one-time hit man. The story sounded preposterous, I told my source. And yet.
Six months later, I found myself speaking with someone else about the UAE government and their use of mercenaries in conflicts around the Middle East and Africa when I asked, on a whim, whether they knew anything about Kushner and bank transfers from a UAE account. My acquaintance grew quiet. Then they replied, “Yes.”
Over the next four years, I came to learn that, sometime in late 2017, the Netherlands Defense Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) made a startling discovery. A General Staff of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation (GRU) operative, a dark web hacker specializing in stolen bank data, was traveling to the UK for an espionage mission. They reached out to the British government for permission to apprehend him when he arrived. The British agreed.
When the Russian national arrived in England, the Dutch informed him that he had two options: he could work for them against the GRU, or the British would arrest him. Once in UK government custody, the operative would be charged with espionage. If convicted, he would spend years in a British prison. The Russian chose to change his employer.
Later that year, the Russian operative gave the Dutch spies access to one of the GRU’s most sensitive assets. Located in Rostov, Russia, the GRU’s hacking and cyber team operated a remote server on which they stored some of their bounty. During their search through these secret files, the Dutch found something astonishing: screenshots of Jared Kushner’s iPhone.
In The Hague, the MIVD hacking team tried to reverse engineer the Russian penetration of Kushner’s iPhone. Kushner owned what was then the latest model, the iPhone X. Released in November 2017, it featured Face ID, a state-of-the-art security feature that Apple had promoted at its launch. The Dutch team had been trying to pick the phone’s door lock, so to speak, when it occurred to them that the Russians may have found an unlocked window to gain entry instead. Their hypothesis was correct. By early 2018, the MIVD had found a vulnerability in the iPhone that gave them access. The security exploit wasn’t perfect, however. Some malware allows a hacker to turn a victim’s phone into a microphone and video camera, turn the phone on or off, and pull and add files. The Dutch solution did not provide that level of access. Instead, when Kushner used the phone, they could see his screen. Almost as soon as they got inside, the intelligence service began capturing every image of Kushner’s screen as he used it, filing their own cache of surveillance on their internal computer servers.
As they monitored Kushner’s phone, they discovered he used it to log in to a UAE bank account. By the time the Dutch spies had visibility into the phone, the account had received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan. Their initial assessment was that the bank account was affiliated with the government there.
For the MIVD hackers, the bank account became an intelligence mystery to unravel. Nearly everything they worked on had a tinge of Russian conspiracy. A little over a year into Trump’s first presidency, the MIVD, like FBI agents and federal prosecutors in Washington working on the Robert Mueller investigation, had only part of the story.
Kushner, UAE ruler Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) and Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) of Saudi Arabia, converged at an auspicious moment. MBS wanted to be crown prince. MBZ wanted to blow up Obama’s Iran nuclear deal, and Kushner wanted both to help him force the Palestinians into a deal that Israel would accept. Despite the perception of his wealth, Kushner was not entirely financially independent of his parents, and the family business, Kushner Companies, faced a billion-dollar loan coming due on their trophy property, the Manhattan office building at 666 Fifth Avenue.
Early in the first Trump administration, MBZ and MBS offered to pay for a slush fund dedicated to helping the new administration with foreign policy goals. The idea was to help pay for Trump’s promised wall between Mexico and the US, for example, in an effort to secure a second term in the White House. The two Arab royals initially discussed with Kushner putting more than $10 billion into the effort. Within months, though, as MBZ pushed the Trump administration to help back MBS’s effort to become his country’s crown prince—and future king—the broader foreign policy slush fund idea fizzled. Instead, MBZ and MBS initially, and then MBZ alone, put at least $2 billion into at least two bank accounts for Kushner. It is unclear how the royals organized their $2 billion in combined payments, but they effectively split the cost. For the purposes of explanation, it is best to understand where and how each bank account was controlled.
Bank account Alpha was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, the largest in the UAE, and was overseen by MBZ’s brother, Tahnoon bin Zayed, who served as the bank’s chairman. Beginning in 2017, the Saudis and Emiratis transferred roughly $750 million into the Alpha account. Alpha would be used as a foreign policy fund. This money would be overseen and partially managed by Kushner and MBZ, who, in their effort to strike a grand bargain to end the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, believed the region’s map needed to be redrawn.
“Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy,” a source who knew of the UAE’s deal with Kushner said. This person held discussions with both senior UAE and Israeli officials about the secret financial arrangement between Kushner, the UAE, and, at least initially, Saudi Arabia. “Jared promised MBZ that he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalization with Israel so that business could take off.” A slush fund—a shared pool of money for off-the-books diplomatic objectives—was a common form of Gulf Arab government corruption, this person explained. “The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent.”
The Alpha account looked like the funding source of a UAE government program, by which MBZ paid his bureaucrats their salaries or funded government-run schools. But how and through whom the money flowed into the Alpha account revealed that it was intended to remain secret, more akin to a covert and illicit scheme, given that it was managed in part by a senior advisor to the president of the United States.
The Dutch spies who monitored the Alpha account noted that all of it was sent by a bank in Azerbaijan in American dollars. Azerbaijan plays a unique role in money laundering. Its central bank maintains high levels of US dollars in its reserves but does not adhere to the highest standards of bank transparency. As a result, Azerbaijani banks have well-established but unadvertised practices of serving as way stations for large transfers, in which a foreign currency is exchanged for an equal amount in dollars. For a roughly 6 to 7 percent fee on the transaction, some Azerbaijani banks will accept a transfer from a client who wishes to move Saudi riyals or Emirati dirhams totaling hundreds of millions of dollars. The Saudi or Emirati client sends the money to the Azerbaijani bank, which then uses a different internal bank account to transfer the equivalent US dollars to the client’s requested destination. For auditors, this shadow trade can’t be discerned.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu vows West Bank military operation after attack kills two Israeli soldiers
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu vows West Bank military operation after attack kills two Israeli soldiers
articles.content_orig:
Diggers were seen demolishing Palestinian homes on Friday afternoon
The Israeli military has begun demolishing Palestinian buildings in the city of Hebron, after two Israeli soldiers were killed in an attack by two Palestinian gunmen.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the military would "destroy" the neighbourhood where the two attackers came from, and that Israel was ready for "extensive action" in the occupied West Bank.
Three other soldiers were wounded in the attack at a checkpoint outside Hebron, before the gunmen were shot dead, officials say.
It comes at a time of high tensions, with extremist Jewish settlers targeting Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, and Israel's general election taking place in four days' time.
Footage verified by the BBC shows an intense gun battle between soldiers and the gunmen. Other footage shows two gunmen exit a car armed with what appears to be a handgun and an assault rifle and start firing on soldiers at the checkpoint, before coming under return fire.
Photos of one of the suspected attackers were shared by AFP news agency
The incident has already begun to influence the ongoing election campaign, with Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - saying that his Likud party would cancel campaign events which had been set for Friday morning.
Speaking later from the scene, Netanyahu said that the military would "demolish this place and completely transform it," referring to the Hebron neighbourhood where the attackers are said to have come from.
It is common for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment.
Netanyahu likened his plans to previous operations in West Bank refugee camps where residential buildings were demolished and thousands were displaced.
He also said he had reviewed plans for the largest military operation in the West Bank in decades - though did not say when it could be carried out.
He added that he had imposed cordons around the city of Hebron - which has around 200,000 residents - and the nearby city of Halhul.
Netanyahu's far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for Israel to launch a campaign in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza or Lebanon," while far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir called for Israel to dismantle the Palestinian Authority.
On Thursday, Foreign Minister Israel Katz accused opposition leaders of undermining the government by criticising Netanyahu's warnings of an attack ahead of the election, saying they would be "responsible" for any future attack on the country.
Opposition chiefs, including frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, offered their condolences to the families of the killed troops and praised those who killed the attackers.
The Israeli military said it had found a large quantity of ammunition in the attackers' vehicle, and that they believe the gunmen had intended to carry out a much larger attack on the nearby Route 35, but ran into the checkpoint - so instead decided to open fire there.
At least 96 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year, according to the UN.
Four Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians there over the same period, the UN says - not including those killed in Friday's attack.

articles.title_orig: Micron Stock Leads Chip Rebound. Dip Buyers Must Buckle Up as AI Chaos Swirls.
articles.title_zh: Micron Stock Leads Chip Rebound. Dip Buyers Must Buckle Up as AI Chaos Swirls.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Some companies don't keep their ambitions secret. They swagger onto the stock market and draw plenty of attention with a splashy IPO and big promises (lookin' at you, Tesla ).
But some incredibly successful stocks are sleeper hits: They quietly sit on the market doing nothing until one day, bam! Their shares take off like a rocket, and everybody wonders how they didn't see it coming.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
That's what happened to memory chipmaker Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) in late 2025: Its shares had languished for years until a global memory shortage and AI data center boom took the stock stratospheric. Between June 25, 2025, and June 25, 2026, the chipmaker's shares grew more than 850%.
If you were lucky enough to invest $10,000 in Micron on that day in 2025, you'd have had $95,370 a year later. Even today, after shares have dropped 25% from those highs, you'd still have $70,970. Not enough, perhaps, to fund a full retirement, but a nice chunk of change.
So, what about right now? Could buying $10,000 in Micron today set you up for life?
It's ironic that even though Micron's share price has grown astronomically since June 2025, its price-to-earnings ratio -- how its share price compares to its profits -- has actually gone down. In June 2025, shares were trading at about 22 times earnings. In June 2026, at its peak, it traded at about 27 times earnings. Today, it's trading at about 12 times earnings.
Why would a wildly successful company that's grown its revenue by 256% and its per-share earnings by 879% in 16 months have a cheaper valuation than it did before?
The simple answer is that the market doesn't expect the good times to last, for two reasons.
The first reason is that this has happened before to memory chip stocks, and it didn't end well. Prices for dynamic RAM (DRAM) memory spiked in 2020-2021 during the pandemic tech-buying surge. After expanding capacity to meet that demand, memory producers wound up with a supply glut, and prices crashed in 2023.
This time around, Micron has tried to protect itself against such a price crash by signing multiyear supply deals with its customers to lock in price floors, allowing it to safely expand its capacity. That's a smart move, but the market is also concerned about competition.
Until now, three companies have had the global market for DRAM and high bandwidth memory (HBM) to themselves: Micron and South Korean companies Samsung Electronics (OTC: SSNLF) and SK Hynix (NASDAQ: SKHY). But all three are planning to expand capacity, while concerns about rapid expansion by Chinese manufacturers abound.
While it's possible that Micron's long-term contracts will allow it to continue to grow revenue and profits, a nervous market is unlikely to give it full credit for its success. It certainly seems doubtful that it will reach a $10 trillion valuation anytime soon (which would turn a $10,000 investment into $100,000).
Even if a $10,000 investment in Micron probably won't set you up for life, the ongoing growth of AI infrastructure deployment should make Micron a solid investment for years to come.

Now that the first folding iPhone has launched, we’ll find out quickly what can go wrong.
The iPhone Duo officially goes on sale today, but a few units already have broken screens. According to posts on Reddit about the affected units, the issue appears to be happening at a similar spot on all of them: Some kind of problem shows up on the inner screen along the hinge and a strange bright line (or lines) across the right side of the display.
Here’s how one user in Australia described what happened to their phone:
Had my iPhone Duo for about six hours and had probably opened it fewer than 20 times.
I was showing it to a friend, and as I opened it, I felt something around the internal hinge, underneath the screen.
As I continued opening it, I heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge.
There were no marks or damage on the inner screen’s surface or the external hinge to suggest anything had been caught or damaged.
The user said that the Apple Store replaced their phone with “a brand-new one on the spot.”
A post showing an image of another broken screen includes a video in a comment demonstrating yet another.
And a separate Reddit thread collected other pictures of affected Duos.
Apple didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: How Can I Hang On To My Digital Life?
articles.title_zh: How Can I Hang On To My Digital Life?
articles.content_orig:
12:36 PM EDT on October 23, 2026
Photo by Sjöberg Bildbyrå/ullstein bild via Getty Images
I've been watching the "available storage" bars on my various digital storage systems creep up over the last couple years with a growing sense of dread. Each percentage point is a tick closer to an upgrade to my package—money I'll have to pay Apple, Google, and Dropbox to continue to store my digital life. Maybe more importantly, I'm aware of just how much stuff I produce every day, and as the mess grows, I wonder if I should do something about it. On worse days, I think maybe I should just succumb to the digital hoarder house I've built for myself.
It is probably my obsession with my own death, paired with the ever-present anxiety about whether the way I spend my days truly matters at all, that has led to an interest in personal archiving practices. My life's work amounts to several terabytes' worth of mp3s, wavs, text files, and jpegs that live on server space I pay to lease somewhere in the world. I like the idea of my work being accessible after I'm gone, and for a long time I trusted the infrastructure of the internet to do that archival work for me. But if the last 20 years have taught us anything, it's that only dummies blindly trust big tech to operate in their best interest.
“"People do not realize how fragile digital media is," said Margot Note, an archivist who specializes in helping individuals and businesses create their own archives. Note told me about bit rot, which is a phenomenon where digital files become corrupted over time from neglect. To get specific: If left alone for too long, the individual bits that make up a digital file can unintentionally flip from 0 to 1 and vice versa, which eventually renders the file unreadable. "Digital files actually require active maintenance. And it's not something that you have to do right away, but over time, they're going to be unreadable." Note suggests to maintain files using two techniques: refreshing and migration. Refreshing refers to routinely moving data from one storage medium to a newer one, like taking a document from a floppy disk and saving it to a newer hard drive.
But there are other, more general concerns about the longevity of digital files. "I don't know if Microsoft Word is going to be around 100 years from now," she said. "You're dependent on the software. You're dependent on the hardware, and you're dependent on corporations that could go out of business. So if you put something in the cloud, you could lose access to it." Migration refers to updating data that was created for obsolete mediums or software into more modern forms, like converting a WordPerfect document to an updated version of Microsoft Word.
Because my specific flavor of neurosis blended with the knowledge that I'm soon going to give birth to a human, I was finally convinced to download Note's book, Creating Family Archives . What I found there was both useful and anxiety-inducing.
"External hard drives, if stored correctly and used sparingly, might last a decade," Note writes. "If not treated well, they may have five years of useful storage life." I thought about my stack of external hard drives sitting in an office drawer, some of which date back to 2010 and which haven't been connected to a computer in at least ten years. I wasn't sure what kinds of files I would find in these old drives, but I hoped that my current MacBook could open the files that were created on a 2008 Dell laptop.
Note refers to the 3-2-1 rule of archiving: Make three copies of something, store it in at least two types of media, and keep one copy at a physically separate location. A practical example: You might keep an album of family photos on your phone, but also consider printing them out (for a second form of media), and storing digital versions on both an external hard drive and in cloud storage (which actually makes four copies, including the printed versions, in at least two physical locations, if you think of the cloud as server space that exists somewhere else in the world).
Here's what I was working with: 58 GB in my personal paid Google Drive, 6 GB in my Defector Google Drive, 3.19 TB in my personal paid Dropbox, 535.45 GB in my paid iCloud, and six external hard drives. The only small bright spot in my current archiving practice is that I store nothing on my computer; after going through enough computer catastrophes, I am religious about saving everything important directly to Dropbox. This gives me some peace, because I know I can switch devices at any point, but it also means my Dropbox is a mess.
Some of the goals I had for this project:
First, I dug out my 8TB hard drive and plugged it in. The last time I used it was in 2020, when I backed up my wedding photos. This was where I hit my first technological roadblock. The hard drive would need to be reformatted before I could add any new data to it, because it had previously been formatted for an older computer I no longer have. Without getting too into the weeds, the hard drive was meant for a PC system, and so each time it connected to a Mac, it had to be formatted specifically for that computer if I wanted to add or remove from it.
This meant that I actually had to delete everything on the hard drive before I could proceed, which would have been a nightmare if I had saved anything more to the hard drive, or had been relying on it as my sole archival source. Luckily, I still had my wedding photos on my Dropbox account, so I could reformat the drive without losing anything (3-2-1 already coming in clutch!). But I could see how this would have posed a much bigger problem if I'd had more stored on this hard drive and didn’t have a system set up to regularly migrate my files.
Once the hard drive was reformatted and writable, I created two folders on it: family-archive and alex-archive. Within each of those folders, I created folders for each year starting in 2016, as well as a "pre-2016" folder for any loose ends that have survived longer than a decade. I followed the naming convention guidelines set out by Preserve This Podcast , which was an archiving project created by the Metropolitan New York Library Council. In order to increase the likelihood that my file names will be readable by future technologies, I kept them all lowercase and replaced spaces with dashes or underscores.
A useful piece of advice Note gave me was to start with my oldest files first. "Those are the most fragile, and then you're gonna forget what those things are as far as what you're looking at," she said.
So I decided to start with my personal Google Drive. I sorted it in chronological order and came face-to-face with 19-year-old me. The oldest document in my drive was from 2011, a writing sample for an internship I ended up getting. There was absolutely nothing special about this piece of writing, which was just the text of an article I'd written for the student newspaper, but I was touched to see evidence of my first ever professional application. I downloaded it and saved it to the pre-2016 folder. Then I deleted it from my Google Drive.
Another important thing Note reminded me was that you are in charge of your own archive. You are not beholden to the morass of stuff you have accumulated over the years. You can delete as much as you want and only archive what matters to you. This archive had two purposes for me: to preserve family photos, videos, and documents; and to preserve my work archive as much as possible. I long ago accepted that the majority of my blogs will probably end up lost to link rot on the internet, but I do want to keep a record of the things I’m most proud of making.
I went through the documents and found grocery lists and spreadsheets of job applications (deleted), but I also found my first awkward attempts at fiction and all the videos from a YouTube series I made about side hustles for a now-defunct feminist blog back in 2015. As I downloaded and saved files, I created new subfolders

articles.title_orig: Everybody panic: A Valve developer said "HLX" in public
articles.title_zh: Everybody panic: A Valve developer said "HLX" in public
articles.content_orig:
Gamers still hoping against hope for a true follow-up to Half-Life 2 (after so, so many years ) may remember last year’s flurry of speculation that Half-Life 3 was finally nearing completion . Amid all those rumors, though, we never got any official sign from anyone inside Valve that a Half-Life project was currently in development.
That changed this week thanks to an apparent slip-up during a panel at GameSoundCon , an industry conference devoted to “the art, technology, and business of game audio.” In a panel devoted to Valve’s use of open audio engines (captured in this Vimeo clip ), Valve composer and audio artist Mike Morasky let an interesting string of three letters slip while talking about the way the company implements high dynamic range (HDR) audio:
Our HDR system is basically that’s one of the three pieces that come together to make an HDR that you can easily optimize. And in fact, I think Deadlock has their own version of HDR. HLX has its own version , so on and so forth [emphasis added].
“HLX,” of course, has been widely reported as the internal code name for Valve’s next Half-Life project. The codename has shown up in Valve engine code since at least 2024 , but it has never been referenced in public by a Valve employee until now (though Morasky was responsible for a close call in an interview last year).
In the panel video, fellow panelist and Valve sound designer David Feise can be seen mumbling a sarcastic “nice work” to Morasky after the HLX codename slips out of his mouth. Later, while the audience is clapping at the end of the Q&A session, Feise leans in to Morasky and appears to say, “Good job—you only said HLX once!”
An official utterance of the “HLX” shibboleth is of course a good sign for those looking for any indication of the franchise continuing beyond 2020’s Half-Life Alyx . But the question of when Valve will make its next Half-Life project official still looms large.
Remember, it was just under a year ago that journalist Mike Straw was adamant that Half-Life 3 would be a Steam Machine launch title . Now that the Steam Machine launch has come and gone without even a nod toward an announcement, we can understand why Valve watchers would be more gun-shy than usual over any new rumors.
Longtime Valve watcher Tyler McVicker—who said Half-Life 3 was in the “final stages of development” and suggested a 2026 announcement was “likely” last year—admitted in a recent video that he now doesn’t believe that HLX is being announced this calendar year. But he also pointed to recently increased coding activity within Valve (as measured by externally viewable internal “commit” numbers) that something big might be coming sooner than later.
One thing is for sure: Whenever Half-Life 3 finally is announced and released, it will have to be truly incredible to make up for the loss of the long-running metagame of speculating about its mere existence .

I have bought NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) on dip after dip, and this latest slide put the stock back at the top of my research list. Shares fell 4.4% in the most recent session and 7.28% over the past month, closing at $212.21. That pullback stands out given NVIDIA's position in AI computing.
My thesis comes down to one point. AI models run on NVIDIA, and the CUDA software layer makes leaving expensive. On the August call, CEO Jensen Huang said "Our position in open models is very good because the CUDA ecosystem is literally everywhere." Developers write for CUDA, clouds rent CUDA, and each new chip generation inherits that installed base. That lock-in strengthens with each chip generation.
First, growth at scale. Revenue for the second quarter of fiscal 2027 reached $96.22B, up 105.8% year over year. Data Center revenue hit $89.02B, up 117%, and networking grew 138%. That tells me customers buy the whole AI factory, chips and connections together. Guidance calls for $108.0B ±2% next quarter.
Second, profitability. NVIDIA runs a 71.07% gross margin, a 60.38% operating margin, and a 101.49% return on equity. Fiscal 2026 free cash flow came in at $96.58B.
The balance sheet and capital return also look strong. Its debt-to-equity stands at 0.073, and interest coverage at 503.42x. NVIDIA returned about $26.0B in Q2 and holds $99.0B of remaining buyback authorization. The 0.019% yield pays me little, so I own this for compounding, and a P/E of 43 looks reasonable for that growth rate.

Broadcom ( NASDAQ:AVGO ) posted AI semiconductor revenue of $16.70 billion, up 221%. Its own filings flag dependence on a limited number of AI customers and significant indebtedness. I prefer NVIDIA's near-debt-free platform.

Brent crude nears $120 as escalating Saudi-Houthi tensions fuel another weekly oil price rally, putting fresh pressure on Trump.
The slow creep of oil prices towards the $120 per barrel mark is a nightmarish scenario for US President Trump, even though there has been little fundamental change in the crude oil markets. A slight drop in freight rates and a ubiquitous flattening of backwardated curves lowered differentials of most grades globally, offsetting some of the pressures coming from higher crude benchmarks. Be that as it may, an escalating Saudi-Houthi conflict paved the way for another 4% weekly gain, with ICE Brent trading around $117 per barrel.

Libya Oil Output Falls After Protests Reemerge. Libya's NOC said unauthorized individuals shut a pipeline valve serving the Hamada and Tahara fields, cutting output by 50,000 and 40,000 b/d respectively, as recurring protests jeopardize crude production that provides 90% of state revenues.

QatarEnergy is seeking additional long-term cargoes from the US and potentially Asia after securing its first agreement with US developer Cheniere (NYSE:LNG), locking in 4 million tonnes of LNG per year until 2054, as domestic LNG outflows remain constrained.

US President Trump declared imported wind turbines and components a national security threat over cybersecurity and foreign dependence concerns, citing a Commerce Department investigation, ordering trade officials to discuss the issue with trading partners.

articles.content_orig:
Update [ Fri 23rd Oct 2026, 5:30pm ]:
While the future of Arkane Lyon seemed precarious following today’s updates, Bloomberg journalist Jason Schreier has followed up with more positive news.
He says there are “multiple paths being explored” to save the studio and he’d “be surprised if it is shut down”.
He does warn, however, that “anything can happen during negotiations”.
Original Story: While the future of former Xbox first-party devs like Double Fine and Undead Labs has already been determined, it’s been a while since we heard word from Arkane Lyon , the studio behind the acclaimed Dishonored games.
Subscribe to Push Square on YouTube 172k
Now an article by Le Monde (paywalled) gives an insight into the struggles of the French studio, as it races to find a buyer before a 13th November deadline.
As you may recall, Microsoft was unable to close the studio immediately due to a consultation period demanded by French law. The Redmond firm is obligated to try to sell the studio, but a mandated three month deadline is now coming to a close.
The team has until 13th November to find new funding, otherwise the studio will be shuttered and around 217 jobs will be lost. According to the report, negotiations are ongoing.
Union representatives claim the team’s current project, Marvel’s Blade – which was announced in 2023 – is “nearing the end of production”. Spokespeople for the studio believe it will be a success if it sees the light of day.
But those same people blame Microsoft for its “disrespectful” treatment of the team.
“We are collateral victims of Xbox’s change in strategy,” one of the people said.
As alluded to above, Microsoft has already shuttered UK studio Ninja Theory , and offloaded various other teams like Compulsion Games et al.
It’s also in the process of reorganising its entire first-party operations, seemingly sunsetting Xbox Game Studios as it places its remaining teams under the umbrella of Bethesda and Activision. Its objective is to focus on big franchises like Fallout and Call of Duty .
The scary part is that the platform holder is not done yet: it’s cut over 1,800 jobs so far, but more redundancies are coming , as it aims to eliminate 3,200 roles overall.

articles.title_orig: Leaked trove reveals extent of far-right AfD’s efforts to court Trump and Maga allies
articles.title_zh: Leaked trove reveals extent of far-right AfD’s efforts to court Trump and Maga allies
articles.content_orig:
Exclusive: Documents show German party’s scramble to request support after president’s 2016 election win and co-leader’s pursuit of Steve Bannon
A data leak from Germany’s far-right German Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has revealed the extent of efforts by the party to court Donald Trump and other leading figures in the Maga movement, stretching back more than a decade.
The trove reveals the pains the AfD took in wooing the president, whom they saw from the beginning as a potential ally, with senior party officials agonising over the wording of an obsequious congratulatory telegram when he was elected in 2016, which included the wish that his “hopes as a person be fulfilled”.
The AfD became a home for anti-immigration voters after 1.2 million refugees arrived in Germany in 2015 and 2016. It entered the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, in 2017 with 12.6% of the vote , came second in the February 2025 federal election with 20.8% , and now leads national polls at about 30% . In September it won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, and it is now trying to form Germany’s first far-right state government since the second world war.
Trump hailed the win in Saxony-Anhalt in a post on his Truth Social, concluding his message with a German version of his Make America Great Again acronym, “MGGA!!!”
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency monitors the party as a suspected rightwing extremist organisation , and state agencies classify five of its regional branches as confirmed extremist .
Its leader in the central Thuringia region, Björn Höcke, was convicted in 2024 of knowingly using a slogan of the SA, the Nazi party’s paramilitary wing. AfD politicians also attended a meeting with extremists at which a mass-deportation “masterplan” was discussed. Its 2025 election programme calls for lifting sanctions on Russia and repairing the Nord Stream gas pipelines programme . Nearly all of Germany’s other parties have kept a “firewall”, refusing to govern with it.
Media outlets including the Guardian have reported on the apparently friendly contacts between the party and the US state department during Trump’s second term.
The leaked documents show AfD officials quickly moving to requests for support from the White House on policy issues when he first won the 2016 election.
Others show a burgeoning political courtship between senior figures including the AfD’s now leader, Alice Weidel, and the key Trump ideologue Steve Bannon.
The data, provided to reporters by the transparency organisation Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), covers more than 420,000 emails, along with documents and personnel records, from the party’s foundation in 2013 to the present, with most coming before 2019.
The AfD said in a statement on Monday that a hosting provider used by the party had been attacked at the end of September and that “only a few mailboxes” had been copied. It told the news agency dpa that most of those mailboxes had not been used for years, and party sources were quoted as saying the published material appeared to be authentic.
AfD figures praised Trump ahead of his first election in 2016, with then leader Frauke Petry calling him a “refreshingly alternative proposition” in the spring of 2016. On the day after Trump won the presidency, Petry said the victory was “encouraging for Germany and for Europe” .
The hacked documents reveal that in the wake of his election, the party scrambled to send an ingratiating telegram to the new president.
Mainstream German politicians greeted Trump’s election with skepticism. On 9 November 2016, the then chancellor, Angela Merkel, offered Trump “close cooperation” only “on the basis of … values” including respect for human dignity “regardless of origin, skin colour, religion, gender, sexual orientation or political views”. The then defence minister, Ursula von der Leyen, called the result a “ huge shock ”. The next day the vice-chancellor, Sigmar Gabriel, reportedly called Trump the “forerunner of a new authoritarian and chauvinist international”, and he counted the AfD among its forces.
On 10 November, Petry emailed the party’s federal board proposing “an official and brief congratulatory telegram to the future US president”. German politics, she wrote, was “once again outdoing itself in politically unacceptable behaviour”; the AfD was “already perceived as the ones who don’t join in the majority howl of the political establishment” and, “as the only German party welcoming a new beginning in the US”, should say so officially.
Eleven of the board’s 13 members replied, all in favour. Current leader Weidel wrote “Yes:-)”. Beatrix von Storch, now deputy leader of the party’s Bundestag group, wrote: “Couldn’t be more of a yes.”
Board member Dirk Driesang added that Trump should also receive, “by post (?)”, the party’s manifesto in English.
The telegram went out on 11 November under Petry’s name, “on behalf of the federal board”, and was released to the press. It told the president-elect: “We are confident that you will readjust the transatlantic relationship and end the wars in Syria and Ukraine by mutual agreement with Russia.”
A second message, for the inauguration, was planned more carefully, and included a concrete request for a political favor. On 11 January 2017, Driesang asked for it to be put on the agenda of the board’s next conference call, “this time faster and better prepared”, and proposed adding a request: “Please support us in our efforts to remove the enemy-state clause from the UN charter.”
The “enemy state” clauses were written into the UN charter in 1945, and exempted action against “any state which during the second world war has been an enemy of any signatory” from the charter’s normal rules, so that the wartime allies could move against any “renewal of aggressive policy” by Germany, Japan or their allies. The general assembly declared them obsolete in 1995 and resolved to repeal them, but the text has never been amended, because changing the charter needs ratification by two-thirds of member states and all five permanent members of the security council.
No German party currently defends the clauses, but the Bundestag’s own research service wrote in 2017 that international lawyers unanimously regard the clauses as having no practical relevance . On the German right, however, the clauses are totemic , and viewed as a limitation on German sovereignty. The AfD’s Bundestag group demanded its deletion in a 2020 motion that called it a “relic of the past” which “indirectly designates Germany an ‘enemy state’”, and every other party voted it down .
AfD’s federal board adopted the enemy state request on its call of 16 January, according to the federal office’s record of the decision contained in the leaked documents.
When the office circulated an English draft on 19 January, Georg Pazderski, then the party’s Berlin leader and a member of its federal board, objected to the tone and to the request for support: “You don’t address the president as Mr Trump, he is Mr President. Otherwise a bit wordy and flowery. I stand by it: the enemy-state clause doesn’t belong in this letter at all. You don’t do that in a letter of congratulation. It looks like a begging letter.”
Driesang replied at 6.16 the next morning: “Personally I of course find the style appropriate, otherwise I wouldn’t have written it that way.”
The office also wanted to know how the telegram should reach Trump: “directly to Trump’s campaign team … or through official diplomatic channels (e.g. the US embassy in Berlin)?”
André Poggenburg, then the party’s leader in Saxony-Anhalt, answered: “all available channels.”
The text released on the afternoon of 20 January, signed by Petry and her then co-leader Jörg Meuthen, kept the request. It told Trump that the clause stood in Germany’s way “as a strange anachronism”, and asked him to see the AfD “as natural allies at your side, because we are the only German party in clear opposition to the wrong pol

articles.title_orig: SpaceX wants to be America's fourth phone carrier — tower owners are cashing in
articles.title_zh: SpaceX wants to be America's fourth phone carrier — tower owners are cashing in
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Elon Musk's SpaceX doesn't just want to beam the internet from space. It wants to sell you a phone plan, and the companies that own the cell towers are already cashing in.
SpaceX ( SPCX ) is in talks for access to at least 80,000 US cell sites, Bloomberg reported Thursday , a step toward building a fourth nationwide carrier .
Crown Castle ( CCI ) is up double digits Friday, with American Tower ( AMT ) and SBA Communications ( SBAC ) close behind. AT&T ( T ) and T-Mobile ( TMUS ) are sliding, and Verizon ( VZ ) is lower too.
The biggest tile on that map is SpaceX itself. At about $2 trillion, it's worth roughly three times all six phone and tower companies combined, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
It's the second time this month the two groups have split this hard. On Oct. 9, SpaceX agreed to pay about $8 billion for a nationwide block of wireless airwaves. Tower stocks jumped, and the carriers sank by double digits that day. Since then, Crown Castle is up 27%, and AT&T is down 14%.
Eighty thousand sites is a big ask. That's about half of the 158,500 cell towers in the US, according to the Wireless Infrastructure Association. American Tower has about 41,000 sites in the US and Canada, and Crown Castle about 40,000.
AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile bring in about 85% of American Tower's US and Canada revenue. For the tower owners, SpaceX would be a new tenant. For the carriers, it would be a new rival.
The market is pricing that in. The carriers have shed about $21 billion in market value Friday, while the tower stocks have added about $9 billion.
Crown Castle CEO Chris Hillabrant didn't name names on Wednesday's earnings call, but he left the door open. "You can assume that we're talking to all parties," he said.
Nothing is signed yet. The talks are still far from a formal lease deal, and some see them as a bargaining chip in SpaceX's dealings with the carriers. Better satellites could also mean SpaceX needs fewer towers than it's asking for.
The next test comes Tuesday, when American Tower reports earnings. Watch whether management talks up SpaceX as a customer, or whether the rally starts to cool.

articles.title_orig: Commission weighs best strategy for new trade talks with China
articles.title_zh: Commission weighs best strategy for new trade talks with China
articles.content_orig:
EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said on Friday that the EU was walking a tightrope in negotiations with Beijing, weighing conventional trade measures against broader political considerations.
After several months of negotiations, Brussels and Beijing reached a deal on 9 October to curb imports of hybrid cars from China. However, the agreement is unlikely to significantly narrow the EU’s record trade deficit with China, which has reached €1 billion a day, a gap the European Commission is seeking to reduce.
“There are whole sectors under threat; each head of states and government is concerned that there might be potential heavy losses of the jobs,” Šefčovič said on Friday, after a meeting of the 27 trade ministers in Ireland.
He added: “We have to proceed not only with the traditional trade techniques, but also with a very political approach, how to balance the trade between between China and the European Union.”
A new round of discussions is taking place at a technical level with Beijing until the end of the year, with political negotiation scheduled for January and March 2027.
But given the urgency, EU leaders gave the European Commission a political mandate last week to work on a “kill switch” tool that would allow Europeans to cut off China's access to their market to counter economic distortions.
Under the October deal, the EU will introduce country-specific quotas allowing 350,000 Chinese hybrid cars onto the European market annually over four years, with a fixed annual adjustment rate of 6%.
The Commission aims to extend the agreement to other sectors, but EU officials warn that progress will also depend on Beijing’s response to the EU executive’s efforts to strengthen its trade defence tools.
The Commission is set to present a new instrument on 9 October aimed at encouraging EU companies to diversify their suppliers of strategic products to reduce their dependence on China.
It also hopes to present a proposal for the so-called “kill switch” that same week and ahead of the December summit of EU leaders. Pushed by France and Germany earlier this month, it would allow the Commission to adopt radical measures against Beijing in the event of economic pressure on the EU market.
Another unilateral EU trade defence measure targeting Chinese chemicals and industrial machinery could also come in December, with the risk of prompting Chinese countermeasures.
According to the latest Chinese customs data, China's exports to the EU have continued to surge, rising by 25% over the past year.

Anthropic’s public listing, which is expected this year at a valuation of as much as $2 trillion, is bound to be a windfall for both early-stage and later-stage investors. But even at the company’s latest private market valuation of $965 billion, the stakes held by many of those VCs and early backers already total billions. Here is what some backers in the leading AI lab are worth at that last round’s price, according to Bloomberg :
Eric Schmidt: The former Google CEO invested in Anthropic’s Series A in 2021, when the startup was valued at $461 million, according to PitchBook data. Today, Schmidt owns about 1% of the company, and even at its current private valuation, his stake is worth nearly $10 billion.
Iconiq: The investment outfit wrote a $6 billion check to Anthropic last year when the company was already valued at $183 billion. That massive late-stage bet is now worth $17 billion and has the potential to double at the IPO.
Menlo Ventures: The VC firm led Anthropic’s Series D and has invested more than $1 billion in the company over time, a stake now worth $14 billion.
Sequoia: The famed VC firm backed the AI lab for the first time only earlier this year, when the company was already valued at $380 billion. The $3 billion investment gave it about 1% ownership, which means it has already more than doubled its investment.
Sound Ventures: The firm, launched by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, invested $35 million in Anthropic’s 2023 Series C round and has since funneled an additional $400 million into the company, resulting in a stake that’s worth billions now. (Kutcher left Sound Ventures this year to launch a new VC firm .)
Spark Capital: The only VC firm known to hold a board seat at Anthropic invested $75 million in that same 2023 Series C round, when it was valued at $5 billion. That position has ballooned more than ninetyfold to $7 billion.

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave Is Down 13% in a Week. Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave Is Down 13% in a Week. Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy
articles.content_orig:
CoreWeave 's ( CRWV -1.19% ) stock has plunged 54% over the past 12 months, and it set a new 52-week low of $53.50 on Oct. 22. In the past week alone, it sank about 13%. Let's see why this neocloud stock fizzled out -- and if it's becoming a compelling buy at these prices.
CoreWeave was once an Ethereum miner, but it repurposed its Nvidia ( NVDA -0.18% ) GPUs to train AI models after the cryptocurrency market crashed in 2018.
Image source: Getty Images.
Today, CoreWeave operates 51 data centers that run over a quarter million Nvidia GPUs to remotely process AI tasks. That streamlined approach enables it to process advanced AI workloads roughly 35 times faster and at 80% lower cost than larger cloud platforms. Its largest customers include Meta Platforms , Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic. Nvidia also owns about 9% of CoreWeave, making it the company's top institutional investor.
CoreWeave went public last March. In 2025, its revenue soared 168% to $5.1 billion, and its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) rose 154% to $3.1 billion. Those explosive growth rates -- driven by the AI market 's breakneck expansion -- dazzled investors, and the stock surged from its IPO price of $40 per share to a record high of $183.58 per share on June 20, 2025.
NASDAQ · As of 2:14 PM ET 10/23/26
At its peak, CoreWeave's enterprise value hit $91.1 billion -- or 18 times the revenue it would generate in 2025. However, it struggled to maintain that premium valuation because investors were concerned about its steep losses and persistent dilution.
Even though its adjusted EBITDA was positive, it posted a net loss of $1.2 billion in 2025. That massive gap was driven by interest payments, equipment depreciation, lease and acquisition costs, and stock-based compensation, all of which were excluded from its adjusted EBITDA.
To stabilize its liquidity, CoreWeave issued more shares and convertible debt. That's why its share count has risen 28% since its IPO, and why it ended its latest quarter with $72 billion in total liabilities and a jaw-dropping debt-to-equity ratio of 14.3. Those glaring weaknesses suggested its business model wasn't sustainable yet, and the Fed's rate hike in September -- its first in three years -- made its messy balance sheet even less attractive.
By the end of the second quarter of 2026, CoreWeave's contracted revenue backlog had grown 246% year over year to $104 billion. For the full year, analysts expect its revenue and adjusted EBITDA to surge 151% to $12.9 billion, with adjusted EBITDA growing 144% to $7.6 billion. But on a GAAP basis, they expect its net loss to widen from $1.2 billion to $2.9 billion.
While CoreWeave's business is booming, it had only 1.85 GW of capacity at the end of June, compared to a contracted backlog of 4.2 GW. It expects to lease more data centers and buy more GPUs to narrow that gap next year, but that expansion will be costly.
For 2027, analysts expect its revenue to grow 106% to $26.5 billion, its adjusted EBITDA to grow 121% to $16.7 billion, and its net loss to narrow slightly to $2.8 billion. At its current enterprise value of $76.2 billion, it trades at just four times next year's sales and six times its adjusted EBITDA. Those low valuations should limit its downside potential, even if near-term concerns about rising rates and steep net losses weigh on its stock.
CoreWeave clearly has a first-mover advantage in the neocloud space ; it's firmly backed by Nvidia, and economies of scale should kick in as its business matures. I didn't love the stock when it skyrocketed after its IPO, but I think it's worth accumulating in the mid-50s -- as long as you can tune out the near-term noise and focus on its long-term growth potential.

articles.title_orig: Many feared trapped as a tall building collapses in Kenya
articles.title_zh: Many feared trapped as a tall building collapses in Kenya
articles.content_orig:
Many people are feared to be trapped in Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, after a multistorey building under construction collapsed, leaving a huge mound of concrete as rescuers dig through the rubble.
The building came down on Friday at about 1pm local time (10:00GMT) on a busy commercial street in Eastleigh, a neighbourhood crowded with thousands of traders and residents.
Nairobi police chief Issa Mohamud said more than 10 upper floors were under construction. The ground floor had been rented to an electronics shop, a butchery and a grocery, according to The Associated Press news agency.
Al Jazeera’s Catherine Soi, reporting from Nairobi, said the developers and authorities are being asked “to answer now” as people were not supposed to be inside a building under construction.
She said rescue efforts were expected to continue through Friday night and Saturday.
Rescuers used poles stripped from trees and excavators to move concrete bound with steel, as heavy equipment was slow to arrive.
Mohamud said one injured woman had been rescued and taken to hospital, while another person who had been calling for help had gone silent. He warned of a potential second collapse because the building was leaning on its neighbour.
Local media reported looting immediately after the collapse and police firing tear gas to disperse crowds.
Joseph Kaula, a plasterer working on the fifth floor of the collapsed building, told AP that he was the last person to walk out.
“The whole area was filled with dust,” he said.
Relatives of those trapped said some had phoned for help immediately after the collapse, but their phones later became unreachable. A tent was set up to report missing relatives.
“Our concern is to save lives,” Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja told reporters.
He said the building had been approved for construction but had no certificate of occupation, so opening shops on the ground floor was illegal.
“This has potentially cost lives,” he told reporters on site.
He said that it was possible “one or two” people had died and that more would be known as time went on.
Kenya’s National Building Inspectorate found that 87 percent of buildings audited nationwide last year failed to meet standards or lacked approvals, according to the AFP news agency.
Sakaja said county governments needed stronger enforcement powers, calling lenient penalties a “slap on the wrist”. Police said they would carry out investigations and anyone found negligent would face the law.

articles.title_orig: The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’
articles.title_zh: The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’
articles.content_orig:
People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans
J ack Price joined the marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on the meter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.
Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”
For generations, buying a first new car has been a rite of passage in the US, the clearest sign of a young person responsibly striking out on their own. But younger millennials and gen Z are increasingly finding that path blocked. The average new vehicle costs more than $50,000, an alarming figure that reflects Americans’ insatiable appetite for progressively larger SUVs and pickups. Meanwhile, adults under 35 are disappearing from showroom floors, accounting for less than 10% of new vehicle registrations in 2024 – a new low.
According to the credit reporting agency Experian, the average monthly car payment in the US is $765 for a new car and $542 for a used one, with the loan terms now stretching to six, even seven, years. A record 21% of new-car buyers pay $1,000 or more a month , according to the autos research group Edmunds. And that’s before factoring in maintenance, fluctuating gas prices and the eye-watering insurance premiums often charged to drivers under 35.
For many young Americans already under the strain of student loans, high housing costs and an unforgiving labor market, buying a new car or even a newer used one is out of the question. Enter the Y2K car – the retro ride that has become a trendy romantic choice for some younger Americans. “There’s definitely a golden era of cars from the late 90s and early 2000s that people just really want all of a sudden,” says Charlie Spears, a service adviser at an independently owned repair shop in Atlanta who conducts prepurchase inspections of used cars on demand. “A lot of people just want something that’s not going to fail them.”
Y2K cars don’t encompass everything produced in that era. They are the ones that simply won’t die. Think wedge-shaped Honda Accords and slab-sided Toyota Camrys: dependable, hand-me-down transport that can last 150,000 miles or more with routine maintenance. (Price’s Jetta, which was built at the end of a model production run that began in 2005, just makes the cut.) They’re economical to run and relatively inexpensive to insure, owing to their drastically lower worth. Best of all, the purchase price is low enough to pay in cash. Even when buyers need a loan – at steep interest rates as modern cars have in effect become mortgage payments on wheels – they can pay it off in a fraction of the time it takes to finance a newer car.
The supply of these bargains is dwindling: used vehicles priced under $15,000, the sweet spot for Y2K cars, have shrunk from 21% of inventory a year ago to 15% , according to industry analysis from Cox Automotive – numbers that speak to the demand for affordable cars. “Part of the draw is the nostalgia factor – people wanting cars they grew up with,” says Consumer Reports’ autos expert Keith Barry. “An old car with the right music on is kind of the closest thing to a time machine.”
On social media, the Y2K car has emerged as an ironic status symbol – a marker of maturity, grit and lack of pretense. Defects – busted aircon, glitchy windows, bits and bobs that have failed, fallen off or been held on with gaffer tape – are simply treated as part of a Y2K car’s personality. “I don’t know what kind of disease that is in the brain,” says one TikTok creator, who has to pry open the fuel door of her 2003 Mitsubishi Outlander with a screwdriver . “But I don’t get frustrated. I’m like, ‘Oh, this is fun.’”
In a Y2K car that takes a lickin’ and keeps on tickin’, creature comforts are beside the point. For many, part of the appeal is the absence of dashboard infotainment displays and other screens that have replaced basic switches and knobs in newer cars, often in the name of cost-cutting. Automakers’ zeal to monetize in-car technology, sometimes charging extra to activate physically installed features such as heated seats and remote start, only reinforces young buyers’ doubts about the value of a new car.
At the same time, do-it-yourself repairs have become harder as cars grow more digitally complex and auto manufacturers cut off access to owners and even independent mechanics . Oftentimes, they require investing in specialty digital readers or computer software to diagnose problems, and bespoke tools for wrenching. Most car owners would sooner punt, take the car to the dealership and pay whatever the maintenance and repair costs – which, of course, is exactly the vertical integration that shareholder-bound manufacturers are after.
Hence the romance with Y2K cars: you can fix ’em yourself, their old-school controls fall easily to hand, they’re tried and tested, seemingly built to last. They just have an aura of invincibility – never mind that their age makes them fundamentally more dangerous and susceptible to frequent repairs. “I’ve used my Jetta as if it were a truck,” Price says. “Transported trees in it, put my surfboard through the sunroof. I’ve done every single thing possible to thrash it beyond its abilities.”
Price’s passengers, however, don’t have much appreciation for Pewter Pebble’s quirks. Often while carpooling to US military installations, senior officers compelled to hold up the sagging headliner would ask him when he was trading in his beater for a new truck or SUV. It was a similar story when Price left the military last year and started chauffeuring Alex Vindman, the Iraq war veteran turned US Senate hopeful, on the campaign trail during Florida’s special election. “I drove him around a couple times in it, and he was like, ‘ What is going on?’” Price says. “The fact that we expect folks who are getting paid, like, a grand a month to have a new car is nuts.”
T wenty-five miles north-west of downtown Atlanta, a half hour’s drive in optimistic traffic, sits Town Center at Cobb, a typical suburban mall in recession. But on the first Sunday of every month, the mall parking comes alive for Caffeine and Octane, a sprawling car show that’s open to the public, free to attend and also has long lines for coffee and donut trucks. And even though the usual turnout of 2,000-plus cars was winnowed down to a few hundred on the gray, showery morning of October’s show, it was still an impressive array of vintage American muscle, Japanese domestic market (or JDM) unicorns and multimillion-dollar exotics. The Y2K cars stood out, too.
Sitting right at the entrance of the show was Anthony DeNaples’s 2000 Buick Regal GS, a sleeper sedan that has become a cult classic. He bought it four months ago for $18,000 on Facebook Marketplace, a price he considered a bargain for such a rare commuter. “Person didn’t really know what they had,” says the 37-year-old custom car builder, who uses the car to ferry his two young daughters. His oldest is constantly goading him to do burnouts, which she calls “making stripes”. Modern cars, he reasons, have become so laden with safety systems – for keeping the car in lane, or slamming on the brakes when sensors detect an obstacle – that they’re less fun to drive hard. “A lot of newer cars, if you want to drive it how it’s meant to be driven,
